title: Timeline and handoff
subtitle: Time buckets, thresholds, and saying only what the evidence says
intro: It is 05:40. Hal still wants Marco's name in the brief. Odalys wants the timeline. You have one query shape left to learn, the one that turns 'seven failures' into 'seven failures inside five minutes', and then you have to write down what you know in a way that survives being read by someone angry.
concepts: Time buckets group by when as well as by whom
A threshold is a question, not a verdict
Hand off facts, hypotheses and gaps separately
recap: Bucket a count by the hour to locate a burst, then by account and five-minute window to identify it
Filter grouped rows with a condition threshold and say what the threshold means
Build an actor's timeline from one key with no event type, and read the absences as evidence
Stack four proven conditions until one record anchors the timeline
Tie every contain, eradicate, recover and harden item to a record, in that order
Hand off facts, hypotheses and gaps in separate columns

missions.title: Failures by the hour
missions.beat: Fourteen failures across twelve hours. Spread evenly, that is a station full of tired volunteers. Bunched, it is something else. Put the failures into one-hour buckets and read the night as a bar chart before you zoom in.
missions.question: How are the fourteen failed logins distributed across the hours of the night?

concept.title: Buckets turn a list into a shape
concept.text: by 1h in the match section groups events by the clock hour they fell in, one row per hour that has any. The first pass over a timeline should be coarse: hours, not minutes. A burst shows up as one row much taller than its neighbours. Then you narrow the window, as the next mission does with five minutes, and the burst resolves into an account and an address.

explain.meaning: A grouping key plus a one-hour window. The key is constant here (every row is FAIL), so the table is one row per hour.
The desk adds this column: the bucket's opening time in UTC.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "FAIL"
match:
  security_result.action by ___
outcome:
  $failures = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $failures desc
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "FAIL"

outcome:

hints: The window is one hour. Durations are a number followed by a unit, with no space.

answer.prompt: How many failures are in the busiest hour (the top row)?

call.prompt: The busiest hour holds more than half of the night's failures; the next busiest holds four, and two hours hold one each. What does the hour view prove, and what does it leave open?

options.label: It proves a password attack in the busiest hour; a bucket that tall on a quiet night needs no further resolution
It shows where to look: one hour is unlike the others. Who failed, from where and how close together is what the five-minute view answers next
It shows the night was ordinary: fourteen failures across four hours is within normal for eleven staff, and the burst is a table artefact

call.why: Coarse buckets locate; fine buckets identify. The 19:00 hour also holds an ordinary mistyped password from Odalys, which the five-minute view separates from the seven that were not.

missions.clue: Eight failures in the 19:00 hour, four in the 22:00 hour, one each at 01:00 and 03:00. The tall bar is the burst plus one stray mistype. The four at 22:00 are Marco's three and one other. The next mission puts a five-minute ruler on the tall bar.

logIt.prompt: Log the hour view as evidence. Time: the whole night as a range. Observation: the 14 FAIL logins fall into four clock hours: 8 in the 19:00 hour, 4 in the 22:00 hour, 1 each in the 01:00 and 03:00 hours. Records: one failure from the 19:00 hour and one from the 22:00 hour (open the rows behind the burst; evt-00039 and evt-00387 are examples). Write the distribution; what it means is for the five-minute view.

missions.caveat: Google's match windows are aligned to the clock in UTC. A burst that starts at 19:58 would be split across two hourly rows; read neighbours together before you call an hour quiet.

missions.title: Failures in five-minute buckets
missions.beat: Seven failures could be spread across an evening or crammed into five minutes. Only one of those looks like a password attack. Group by account and by five-minute window, and keep buckets with more than three failures.
missions.question: Which account had more than three failures inside one five-minute window?

concept.title: Time buckets
concept.text: by 5m in the match section adds the clock to the grouping key: one row per account per five-minute slice. The buckets are fixed on the clock (19:05 to 19:10), not sliding, so a burst that straddles a boundary can be split. condition then filters the groups, the way a filter section filters events.

explain.meaning: A placeholder. It names the field so match and outcome can refer to it.
Group by account and by five-minute bucket. over every 5m means the same thing.
Keep only groups whose calculated failures exceed three.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "FAIL"
$account = principal.user.userid
match:
  $account by 5m
outcome:
  $failures = count(metadata.id)
condition:
  $failures > 3
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "FAIL"
$account = principal.user.userid

hints: Run it. The window_start column is the bucket's opening time.
Remove the condition section and run again to see every account's buckets.
One row: pledge-desk, bucket starting 19:05, seven failures.

call.prompt: Google's documentation is inconsistent about condition in Search: one page documents it, two comparison tables say Search does not use it. What should you do before relying on this shape at work?

options.label: Assume it works in production because this trainer accepts it and the syntax parsed
Run it once in your own tenant and keep the result; docs describe, tenants decide
Never use condition anywhere; read every table by eye and filter rows in a spreadsheet

call.why: This trainer follows the page that documents outcome conditions in Search. Your tenant is the authority. The query also works without the condition section; you simply read the table yourself.

missions.clue: pledge-desk, 19:05 to 19:10, seven failures, all from 198.51.100.23. Marco's three failures at 22:41, 22:42 and 22:44 land in one bucket too, but three is not more than three. Change the threshold and watch him appear; then ask whether that makes him a suspect or a man who forgot he was fired.

logIt.prompt: Write a Harden item: lock out after more than three failures in five minutes on VPN-GW-01, require MFA on the VPN, and retire the shared pledge-desk account in favour of named accounts. Answers: your burst evidence. Owner role: IT lead. Urgency: this week. Harden items become the proposed controls in the handoff.

missions.caveat: Search statistics have a 90-day lookback and a results cap; the time range picker on the Search page, not the query, sets the window being bucketed.

missions.title: Lower the bar, read the difference
missions.beat: Hal says 'three failed logins from the fired guy is enough'. Set the threshold to three or more and look at both rows side by side before you answer him.
missions.question: At three or more failures per five minutes, how many account-buckets appear?

concept.title: A threshold is a question, not a verdict
concept.text: Thresholds decide what you look at, not what is true. Lowering one adds rows; each added row deserves the same scrutiny as the first. Here the second row is a disabled account failing from the room its owner used to work in, with 'Account disabled' in the summary.

explain.meaning: Greater than or equal. Equivalent to > 2 for whole numbers; both forms pass.
Click into the events behind each row and read it. The summary explains the failure.

answer.prompt: How many rows does the table have now?

call.prompt: Marco's row: three failures, 22:41 to 22:44, Studio B, 'Account disabled', no success after. pledge-desk's row: seven failures from outside, then success, then the playout PC. What goes in the brief about Marco?

options.label: Marco attacked the station; three failures from a fired host in his old studio are enough to name him in the brief as the intruder
Omit Marco entirely; failed attempts against a disabled account are not a finding, and a line about him would only inflame the board
Marco tried a disabled account from Studio B at 22:41; nothing succeeded and nothing follows. Recommend HR follow-up, not attribution

call.why: It is a real finding and it is not the intrusion. Writing it precisely protects the station and protects Marco from a story the evidence does not support.

missions.clue: Two rows, two different nights. One is an intrusion. The other is a man who walked into his old studio at 22:40 and tried his old password three times. Both belong in the brief; only one belongs in the incident.

logIt.prompt: Log a Hypothesis, status refuted: Marco Vela carried out the intrusion. Contradicting refs: your burst evidence (an outside address, not Studio B), your click evidence (the password left through Hal's desk) and your playout evidence (pledge-desk, not marco.vela). Marco's building access a week after he was let go is a Gap for the station, if you want to add one.

missions.caveat: Why did Marco have building access a week after being let go? That is a finding for the station, not for this query.

missions.title: Everything from one address
missions.beat: Build the attacker's own timeline in one query. Drop the event type entirely and ask for every event, of any kind, whose principal.ip is 198.51.100.23. Then read what is there, and what is not.
missions.question: What does the outside address appear in tonight, across every event type?

concept.title: A timeline is one filter with no event type
concept.text: Most queries start with metadata.event_type. A timeline query leaves it out on purpose: one key, every event type, in time order. The absences are evidence too. If an address appears only in logins, the actor did not run processes or make connections as that address; after the login they are someone else in the logs, an internal host and an account, and the timeline continues under that key.

hints: One condition and nothing else: the attacker address in principal.ip. No event type, so every type is searched.

answer.prompt: How many events carry that principal.ip, of any type?

call.prompt: Every row is a USER_LOGIN through VPN-GW-01; there is no process, DNS or connection event from the address. Why, and what does the timeline do next?

options.label: The sensors missed the attacker's traffic, so the network and endpoint logs for the night are incomplete and must be flagged as a gap before anything else
After the VPN login the actor is inside: their activity is logged under the internal host AUTOMATION-01 and the account pledge-desk, so the timeline pivots to those keys
The address only ever guessed passwords; the success at 19:21 was a coincidence by a legitimate user, and the attacker never got past the gateway

call.why: An outside address stops at the gateway. From 19:30 the same actor is 10.9.4.40 and pledge-desk in every other log; the timeline is one story told under three keys, and the handoff should say which key applies when.

missions.clue: Eight events, all logins, 19:05:10 to 19:21:04. Then silence from that address, because the attacker no longer needed it: from 19:30 they are pledge-desk on AUTOMATION-01. The timeline changes key and keeps going.

logIt.prompt: Add a Timeline entry. Time: 19:21. Fact: 198.51.100.23 appears in eight events tonight, all USER_LOGIN through VPN-GW-01 as pledge-desk, seven FAIL from 19:05:10 and one ALLOW at 19:21:04; it appears in no other event type. Evidence ref: the # of your burst evidence. Write the absence as part of the fact.

missions.caveat: In a tenant, the same timeline would include the gateway's own flow records and possibly the attacker's address in target.ip for responses. The grouped field ip would catch both roles.

missions.title: Capstone: when did they get in?
missions.beat: Last query. The burst ended at 19:09:50. Find the first successful login for the shared account after it, from the same outside address, and read the exact time. That timestamp anchors the whole timeline.
missions.question: At what time did pledge-desk first sign in successfully from outside?

concept.title: Four conditions, one row
concept.text: Every condition you add removes rows. Login, allowed, the shared account, the outside address: four facts you already proved, stacked until one record is left. When a filter lands on exactly one row, that row's timestamp is the anchor every incident timeline needs: everything before it is the lure, everything after it is the attacker's hands on the station.

hints: Four conditions: login, allowed, the shared account, and the outside address you found in chapter 1.
Add principal.ip = "198.51.100.23" to the allowed-login filter for pledge-desk.

answer.prompt: Time of that first success (HH:MM, UTC)?

call.prompt: Odalys asks: 'So who did it?' What is the honest answer?

options.label: Someone using the pledge-desk credential from 198.51.100.23, obtained via the 18:40 phishing email that Hal's workstation visited. The person is unidentified
Hal did it: his desk resolved the domain, his inbox got the lure, the shared account is the one he uses at the pledge desk, and he was in the building all night
Marco did it: he knew every password on the pier, he had a motive, he was in Studio B at 22:40, and he failed three logins the same night

call.why: The logs identify an account, an address and a sequence. They do not identify a human. Saying so is the difference between an analyst and a rumour.

missions.clue: 19:21:04. Eleven minutes after the last guess. Nine minutes before the playout PC. The whole night hangs on that one second, and you can show it.

logIt.prompt: Write the Determination: confirmed incident, confidence high. Deciding refs: the burst and the 19:21:04 success, the click, the PledgeSync folder and the upload. Summary, two sentences: an outside party used the pledge-desk credential, taken through a lookalike sponsor portal, to persist on AUTOMATION-01, take the donor list and air the 03:10 segment. The person is unidentified; Marco's attempts failed against a disabled account.

missions.caveat: Timestamps are UTC here. Real sources mix zones and clock drift; normalize before you build a timeline.

missions.title: Contain, eradicate, recover, harden
missions.beat: 05:55. Before the handoff, the plan. Odalys needs four lists, each item tied to a record someone can reopen: what to cut off now, what to remove, what to put back, and what to change so it does not happen on the next pledge night. Read the four lists against the evidence that justifies them.
missions.question: Which remediation goes in which list, and which evidence does each item answer?

concept.title: Every action answers a record
concept.text: Containment stops the bleeding and buys time; it is justified by what is still happening. Eradication removes what the attacker left; it is justified by what you found. Recovery puts the station back on air; it is justified by what was damaged. Hardening changes the conditions that let the night happen; it is justified by how the attacker got in. An item with no evidence reference is an opinion, and a list with one missing phase is a plan that will be rerun.

explain.meaning: Block egress to 203.0.113.0/24 at the gateway (the beacons were still running at 05:50: cadence evidence, first and last lookups). Isolate AUTOMATION-01 from the network (the task fires every ten minutes: PledgeSync evidence). Reset the pledge-desk password and end its sessions (the credential is in use from outside: burst evidence, 19:21 success).

Disable and remove the PledgeSync task and sync.ps1, stage.bin and the staged files in C:\ProgramData\PledgeSync (task event evt-00141, the curl launch, the folder evidence). Remove the lure from the two inboxes that did not click (lure evidence: odalys.reyes and the pledge-desk mailbox). Treat the encoded command as unknown until decoded (the -enc Gap).

Rebuild AUTOMATION-01 from a known-good image rather than cleaning it, restore the schedule and verify the 06:30 news airs (the --inject launch and segment.wav). Tell the donors whose names were read on air, and the board, what left the building: the 48 MB upload five minutes after donors_export.zip (upload evidence). Confirm Dez's 20:15 restart with Dez and close that Gap.

MFA and lockout after more than three failures in five minutes on VPN-GW-01 (burst evidence). Named accounts in place of the shared pledge-desk login (the account-is-not-person Gap). PowerShell script-block logging and an alert on hidden plus encoded (the 19:33 launch). An egress allowlist for the playout PC (cadence evidence) and partner-domain allowlisting at the mail gateway (lure and real-sponsor evidence).

Contain before eradicate: removing the task while the credential still works invites it back. Eradicate before recover: a rebuilt machine that keeps the shared password is a rebuilt target. Harden last and longest; its items become the handoff's proposed controls.

call.prompt: Dez offers to delete the PledgeSync task right now, before anything else, because it is the thing that keeps calling home. What is the right call?

options.label: Let him; eradication is the fastest way to stop the beacons, and the password and the gateway block can follow once the task is gone
Wait for the morning and the full board before touching anything, since changing the machine now would destroy evidence the investigation still needs
Contain first: block the range and reset the shared password, then remove the task; a working credential would let the task be recreated the moment it is deleted

call.why: Order is part of the plan. The task is a symptom of a credential that still works and a path that is still open; close those, then remove what they left. Preserve the task definition and the folder before deletion for the record.

missions.clue: Four lists, every item pointing at a record. Odalys reads the Contain list first and reaches for the phone. The rest of the plan survives the morning because each line says why.

logIt.prompt: Write a Recover item: rebuild AUTOMATION-01 from a known-good image and verify the 06:30 news airs on schedule, then notify the donors whose names were read on air and the board about the donor list that left at 02:10. Answers: your upload evidence and your PledgeSync folder evidence. Owner role: station manager with the volunteer engineer. Urgency: today.

missions.caveat: Real incident response follows the organisation's plan and its legal and notification duties. The four lists are the shape; the content and the order of notification are decided by people with authority you do not have at 05:55.

missions.title: Handoff
missions.beat: 06:05. Odalys has coffee for both of you and a legal pad. Hal is in the doorway. You have the pad. Write the three columns every handoff needs: what the logs show, what you believe and why, and what you could not see.
missions.question: What goes in the brief, and in which column?

concept.title: Facts, hypotheses, gaps
concept.text: Facts are things a second analyst could reproduce from the same queries. Hypotheses are the story that explains the facts, labelled as such. Gaps are what you lacked: the email body, the decoded command, the server at 203.0.113.44, Dez's confirmation. Mixing the columns is how good investigations become bad decisions.

explain.meaning: 18:40 three lure emails from pier9-partners.example. 18:52 PLEDGE-DESK-02 resolved and connected to 203.0.113.44. 19:05 to 19:09 seven pledge-desk failures from 198.51.100.23. 19:21:04 success. 19:30 to 19:36 pledge-desk on AUTOMATION-01: run-as svc-playout, encoded PowerShell, task PledgeSync, sync.ps1. 19:40 to 05:50 ten-minute beacons. 01:58 to 02:10 donor spreadsheet compressed and 48 MB sent to 203.0.113.44. 02:58 to 03:02 segment.wav written and injected into the 03:10 slot. 22:41 to 22:44 marco.vela three failures, account disabled, Studio B.
The pledge-desk password was entered into the fake portal from Hal's desk. The donor list was the content of the 48 MB upload. The broadcast was intended to be noticed.
No email body or attachment analysis. Encoded command not decoded. No visibility past 203.0.113.44. Dez's 20:15 restart assumed benign pending his confirmation. Marco's building access unexplained.

Confirmed incident, high confidence. An outside party used the shared pledge-desk credential, taken through a lookalike sponsor portal, to persist on AUTOMATION-01, exfiltrate the donor list and air the 03:10 segment. The person is unidentified; Marco's attempts failed against a disabled account.

Contain: block egress to 203.0.113.0/24 and isolate AUTOMATION-01. Eradicate: disable the PledgeSync task and sync.ps1, reset the pledge-desk password, remove the lure from the two unclicked inboxes. Recover: rebuild AUTOMATION-01 and verify the 06:30 schedule, tell the donors whose names aired. Harden: MFA and lockout on VPN-GW-01, named accounts instead of pledge-desk, PowerShell logging, an egress allowlist for the playout PC.

Problem: a phished shared credential reached the playout PC and persisted there. Assets: AUTOMATION-01, PLEDGE-DESK-02, pledge-desk, svc-playout. Controls: the Harden list. Detections: more than three failures in five minutes on one account from one outside address; hidden plus encoded PowerShell from a non-admin account; a scheduled task created minutes after a new login; one outbound connection over 10 MB to a newly seen address. Acceptance: each rule fires on tonight's records replayed and stays quiet on a normal night. Open: the decoded command, the server behind 203.0.113.44, Dez's confirmation, Marco's building access.

call.prompt: Hal asks you to add one line: 'Marco Vela is the primary suspect.' Which response is correct?

options.label: Add it; the board asked for a name, the treasurer is the one who will read the brief first, and the logs do not rule Marco out of the building that night
Decline: the evidence places the intrusion on a shared credential used from outside after a phishing email, and shows Marco's attempts failed against a disabled account
Add it as a hypothesis, clearly labelled, so the brief keeps the peace without stating it as a fact, and let the board decide what weight to give it

call.why: A hypothesis still has to explain the facts. 'Marco did it' explains none of them and contradicts several. The brief's job is to be right, not to be comfortable.

missions.clue: Odalys reads the pad twice, resets the pledge-desk password, pulls the playout PC off the network, and calls the board. Hal sits down. The morning news goes out at 06:30, on time, with no static.

logIt.prompt: Write the Handoff ticket. Press Assemble from casebook to pull the problem statement, refs, controls and open questions from your other tabs, then write the rest yourself. Affected assets: AUTOMATION-01, PLEDGE-DESK-02, the pledge-desk and svc-playout accounts. Detection ideas, in words: more than three failures in five minutes on one account from one outside address; hidden plus encoded PowerShell from a non-admin account; a scheduled task created minutes after a new login; one outbound connection over 10 MB to a newly seen address. Acceptance criteria: how the engineer proves each control works. This ticket is where a Cybersecurity Engineering course picks up.

missions.caveat: This case is fiction. The habit is not: facts, hypotheses, gaps, every time.
